So this is something I spend a lot of time thinking about. This is known as the free-rider problem. When trying to improve a system, we don't want people taking advantage of loopholes, because it is a drain on others, and makes the system as a whole less efficient. This fact should be fairly self evident, and is reasonable that it upsets normal people.

When designing algorithms for software, you often encounter the free-rider problem. In terms of software, there may be calculations that take a lot of time, or paths to explore that are a waste of computational effort. You may need to update nodes or objects that don't require it, before getting to the one that is needed. However, the interesting bit is that in many sufficiently complex environments, it takes more computational effort to avoid these 'free-riders' than to just ignore them and pretend its not an issue. For a search algorithm, you can sometimes get the efficiency down to O(n*log(n)) when you ignore the free riders, but it becomes O(n^2) if you actively ignore them.

If we provided higher wages, sure, someone may demand more from welfare, but that person may be able to afford a higher standard of living and be less of a drain on the police system, or less of a drain on medicade, or less of a drain somewhere else. What increasing the minimum wage really does is force employers to pay a more "fair" wage.

I use "fair" with air quotes because there are only two objective measures of a fair wage - everyone makes the same amount, or everyone makes whatever the market will bear. In reality there's no such thing as a free wage - our consumer economy could not survive with the quickly shrinking labor demand in a true free market, and while an egalitarian economy may sound ideal to some people, I think most people would consider it unfair.

Some companies went ahead and choose to boost wages to $10.10 from $7.50 immediately instead of slow increments over 5 years. Some of the employers that did this were fairly menial jobs. A lot people decided to fuck their old job and went to do an easier job for more money. Businesses were already giving people shitty hours so that wasn't affected. About 1 year in, the labor pool got emptied of good employees and businesses that needed skilled labor couldn't get it because their wage was unattractive. Year 2, wages started to rise and now you are much more likely to see skilled labor positions starting at $15-$20 an hour. Our community is only about 50,000 so when a few large employers hiked their wages, it added a lot of disposable income to the area. Lot of shops and small businesses have popped up and some people choose to make more money with their extra money. New shops often add more jobs and pay competitively so they can attract reliable employees. People still hire the shitty workers too, they just give them really low hours and use them as backup. While driving home from Origins, I had a breakthrough for a new game idea. Jason, my copilot, and I hashed out some theory behind the main game mechanism, and I spent several hours researching the math behind it (similar to that of Spot it). The name Fano-bots comes from the mathematician Fano, who worked with finite projective planes.

(Basically, players match symbols on their cards to collect robot pieces, for reasons that have yet to be solidified)

Jason was gracious enough to whip up some cards for the first prototype, and we played Fano-bugs at the inaugural meeting of our resurrected game design group.

Obviously the thing broke after a few minutes. For starters, I only had one copy of each component - and everyone collects a component each turn! Yikes...

Fast forward to the third game design meetup - last night. Since the first meetup, I have learned (roughly) how to use Inkscape and whipped up some terrible looking robots! https://veuwer.com/i/2x9v

But at least it played last night. I still have no idea what the robots DO, or why you would want one component (or completed robot) over another.

Anyone else working on anything?
I've been working on designing a game: "Fano-bots"

This is incredible and something I would like to start doing.

Besides telling you that I can't wait to see your progress, I wanted to say I think it's a good idea to post in existing subs to expand the communities before branching out into more specific subs.

it's a good idea to post in existing subs to expand the communities before branching out into more specific subs.

Makes sense. I've never really been involved in the early stages of a community (well - besides a local airsoft forum, but that's different!), so that's good to know.

As for the design, I'm thrilled to just have something playable, after a year or so of feeling stale. (Truth be told, the process of developing my first published game proved to be very draining, and it has taken a while to get my mojo back)

One of my weaknesses in the last 1-1.5 years has been my inability to MAKE A PROTOTYPE. Part of it was being surrounded by so many graphic design gurus - anything I would do would be of embarrassing quality compared to their alpha prototypes.
Another contributing factor is my strength at developing/improving existing games. I am proud and honored to have been included in the playtests of several successful published games, but even the designer credit in "my" game was really a result of me developing the game so much with Jason.

Anywho. So there's a playable game! Awesome!

The "getting robot parts" mechanism is more clever than fun (the math is slick), which kinda sucks. And it's more fun than meaningful (the decisions are sometimes lacking), which can be another big error.

So we'll see. In all of this, it's really easy to lose sight of the goal of the game - the reason for its existence. I want a game that both my mom (Farkle, Sequence, Oh Hell, Rummy, and Ticket to Ride fan) and my game group will enjoy.
I want the rules to be simple, elegant, and memorable.
I want the setup to be short.
I want the actions and mechanisms to be somewhat integrated with the theme.
And I want it published by one of 3-4 small publishers that I know reasonably well :)
